title: Why I Will and Won’t Care if Michigan Legislators Block Funding for CCSS Implementation
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing as Michigan legislators moved to defund Common Core implementation, Stuart separates what he would and would not lose. He would not much care, because his district has committed to the standards regardless, and because his teaching answers to long-term student flourishing rather than to whatever the state mandates. He still defends the CCSS as a real improvement on the old subject-siloed 'wish list' standards: short enough for colleagues to read together and pare down, and a shared cross-content language for literacy. He would care, though, because the anti-Common Core campaign runs on misinformation and scaremongering, and because the legislature is throwing out the standards along with the high-stakes tests attached to them. His central distinction is that the standards are not the problem but the tests are, and he would happily defund Smarter Balanced until it is proven reliable and valid. He closes by recasting his blog community as being about doing education better rather than about any single standards document.
points: Stuart's governing principle is that a teacher's mission of long-term student flourishing comes before any state or standards mandate, which is why a state reversal would change little in his classroom.

He defends the CCSS on practical grounds: unlike the state's earlier sprawling lists, the anchor standards can be read in one sitting by a team of colleagues and narrowed to something focused enough to work.

His sharpest move is to decouple the standards from their assessments, supporting common assessments in principle while opposing high-stakes, time-consuming tests that give teachers no usable information.
He treats the online Common Core fight as a literacy problem in its own right, noting that critics who claim a hidden agenda go silent when asked to point to it in the text.
quotes: While I'm the first person to point out the shortcomings of the CCSS (e.g., there are still too many of them; too few teachers and administrators have actually read them, partly because they are too long; they seem destined to be bound to highly expensive standardized tests), they are, as a whole, a vast improvement on the wish list, subject-separated standards of the past. In the Common Core, we have a shared language across content areas for improving the verbal competence (i.e., literacy) of our students.

Secondly, I've never much cared about standards or what the state does in terms of them. As a teacher, I am about promoting long-term student flourishing; in other words, I want my students to live choice-filled lives. This driving mission will always come before what the state or standards dictate.

Frankly, the Common Core just makes a helluva lot more sense to me than the behemoth standards wish lists that my state produced on its own. I can wrap my head around the Common Core; I can read the anchor standards in a sitting with a group of colleagues, and together we can pare them down into something focused enough to really work.
I have had commenters tell me that the Common Core advances a left wing agenda to brainwash my kids. When I ask them where that agenda is evidenced in the standards document, they are silent.

I see the value in common assessments across departments, districts, and even states and the nation. The objective, comparative information they can give us is valuable for improving our craft. But when the assessments are high stakes, when they take up an inordinate amount of time, and when they don't yield valuable information for teachers and students… well, then they don't make sense and aren't worth the billions spent on them.
The standards aren't the problem; the tests are. The standards just set some great goals for college/career readiness. Why throw them out?

We don't always agree on everything, but we damn well agree on the importance of doing education better. We agree that long-term student flourishing is a worthy goal. And, in general, we agree that large amounts of reading, writing, thinking, and talking are a great way to get there.
